snip.t: Bronchiectasis is permanent, abnormal dilatation of the bronchi with chronic inflammation and infection, leading to a clinical syndrome of chronic productive cough, recurrent chest infections and sometimes haemoptysis.

Bronchial arterial supply – systemic bronchial arteries run alongside bronchi: Chronic inflammation induces neovascularisation; fragile bronchial vessels are the source of haemoptysis when they rupture.

Transmission occurs when a person inhales droplet nuclei containing M. tuberculosis, and the droplet nuclei traverse the mouth or nasal passages, upper respiratory tract, and bronchi to reach the alveoli of the lungs.

•There is no direct sympathetic innervation of the smooth muscle of the bronchi, and antagonism of parasympathetically induced bronchoconstriction is critically dependent upon circulating epinephrine (adrenaline) acting through β2- receptors on the surface of smooth muscle cells.

Trachea and main bronchi – cartilaginous rings keep airway patency; mucosa lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells.: Inflammation targets this epithelium; loss of ciliary beat and excess mucus → cough and sputum production.

Submucosal mucous glands (seromucous) – located in the larger bronchi; normal Reid index ≈ 0.4.: Chronic irritation causes gland hypertrophy → Reid index > 0.5, the hallmark of chronic bronchitis; explains persistent mucus hypersecretion.

Bronchial tree (segmental bronchi, bronchioles): Aspiration deposits bacteria into dependent bronchi; obstruction (tumour, mucus plug) creates stasis, allowing anaerobic proliferation and tissue necrosis.

qs.q: A chronic smoker presents with a productive cough for over three months in each of two consecutive years. Which histological measurement is expected to be increased in the bronchi of this patient?
qs.e: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically and characterized pathologically by mucus gland hyperplasia, which is quantified by an increased Reid index. The FEV1/FVC ratio is decreased in obstructive lung diseases rather than increased.

qs.q: A patient with cystic fibrosis presents with copious purulent sputum, digital clubbing, and recurrent respiratory infections. Imaging reveals permanent dilation of the bronchi due to destruction of smooth muscle and elastic tissue. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Bronchiectasis involves permanent dilation of bronchi caused by destruction of muscle and elastic tissue from conditions like cystic fibrosis or recurrent infections. Emphysema features permanent airspace enlargement distal to the terminal bronchiole rather than bronchial wall destruction.

qs.q: A previously healthy 5-year-old girl has fever, expiratory wheezes, and suddenly worsening dyspnea. WBC is 14,480. Emergency bronchoscopy reveals bronchi plugged by exudates. Most likely organism?
qs.e: High WBC + bronchi plugged by fibrin-rich neutrophilic exudates in a child after descending laryngotracheobronchitis = Haemophilus influenzae. Can cause bronchopneumonia with airway obstruction.

qs.q: A 41-year-old woman has episodic dyspnea with expiratory wheezes, elevated serum IgE, peripheral eosinophilia, sputum eosinophils, perihilar bronchiectasis on CXR, and detectable serum galactomannan. Most likely pathologic finding in her bronchi?
qs.e: Elevated IgE + eosinophilia + galactomannan (Aspergillus cell wall component) + bronchiectasis + asthma exacerbations = allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). The fungus colonizes bronchi non-invasively.

es.q: An autopsy reveals significant submucosal gland hypertrophy in the bronchi, with the Reid Index measured at 0.6. Identify the chronic airway disease indicated by this finding and briefly explain the significance of the Reid Index value.
es.m: This finding indicates **chronic bronchitis**. The Reid Index measures the thickness of the submucosal glands relative to the total thickness of the bronchial wall. A value greater than 0.4 (as seen with 0.6) signifies significant submucosal gland enlargement, which is characteristic of chronic bronchitis and contributes to excessive mucus production and airway obstruction.

es.q: A pathologist receives a lung biopsy from a patient with a history of chronic productive cough. Microscopic examination reveals significant submucosal gland enlargement in the bronchi. What quantitative index would be used to assess this finding, and what value indicates significant enlargement?
es.m: The Reid Index is used to assess submucosal gland hypertrophy in chronic bronchitis. A Reid Index of >0.4 indicates significant enlargement.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The bronchi are the main airways branching from the trachea into the lungs, delivering air to alveoli. Their structure and innervation influence cough, mucus clearance and susceptibility to infection.

sections.p: Bronchi are the primary conduits for air from the trachea to the lungs, branching into smaller airways that end in alveoli. Their anatomy underpins respiratory function and disease.
The trachea divides at the carina into the right and left main bronchi. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical, making it a common site for aspiration.
The bronchi lie posterior to the trachea, anterior to the esophagus and vertebral bodies, and are surrounded by pulmonary arteries and veins.
b: Right main bronchus passes behind the right main pulmonary artery

sections.p: Each bronchus receives arterial supply from the bronchial arteries (branches of the thoracic aorta) and venous drainage via bronchial veins into the azygos system.
Sympathetic fibers from the cervical sympathetic chain and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve innervate the bronchi, regulating bronchial tone and mucus secretion.
Bronchi conduct air, filter debris via mucociliary escalator, and regulate airflow through bronchoconstriction or dilation.
b: Mucus glands secrete mucus for trapping particles

sections.p: Bronchial pathology includes bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and foreign body aspiration. Clinically, bronchial obstruction leads to wheeze, cough, and infection.

sections.p: Remember the right main bronchus is more vertical and wider, making it the common site for aspiration. In bronchiectasis, look for a ‘tram‑track’ sign on imaging.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent high fever with productive cough

faq.a: Chronic infection, obstruction, or immune deficiency leading to permanent airway dilation.
Chest X‑ray, CT, and bronchoscopy reveal narrowed or blocked airways.

faq.q: Why is the right bronchus more prone to aspiration?
faq.a: Its vertical orientation allows foreign material to travel more easily into the lung.
